Your agents put apps on your iPhone through aOS. When there is no connection, installs wait until the iPhone is on any Wi-Fi.
aOS sends a routine into its session on the Mac when it is due and Claude Code isn\'t busy. If the Mac was asleep, it comes up to 6 hours later.
Five fields in the Mac\'s time, like 0 6 * * 1-5 (Monday to Friday at 6:00); several separated by ;.
For this routine only. Afterwards the session goes back to its own model and effort.

On the Mac: click aOS in the menu bar, then “Pair” next to iPhone. aOS uses the Mac\'s Remote Login for this, nothing else.
This phone makes its own key. Only its public half goes to the Mac.

Approving a sign-in always needs your fingerprint, face or screen lock, whether or not the app itself is locked.
Turn on the lock for aOS
Sign-in requests and help requests that come while aOS is in the background, as long as it is still connected.
Messages aOS sends into its session on the Mac on a schedule, for example a briefing every morning.
Pinned at pairing. If the Mac answers with another key, the app stops and tells you.
Scan a new pairing code of this Mac, for example after it was set up again.
This phone forgets the Mac. To remove the phone\'s key from the Mac too, open aOS on the Mac and remove it from the paired devices.
Sign-in requests and help requests from this Mac no longer reach this phone.
To log in to another computer with this phone\'s key, add this line to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys there. The public key isn\'t secret.
The private key was made in this phone\'s secure hardware and can\'t leave it.
The private key is in this phone\'s keystore without secure hardware and is never synced.
The private key was made in this computer\'s TPM and can\'t leave it.
Windows keeps the private key for your user account and doesn\'t let it be exported. It is never synced.
The private key is in a file only your user account can read, encrypted with a key in your keyring. It is never synced.
The private key is in a file only your user account can read. No keyring (Secret Service) was found to encrypt it. It is never synced.
They stay in your Bitwarden account. aOS on your Mac signs in to it with Bitwarden\'s own command line tool; this phone never talks to Bitwarden.
A sign-in request shows which of your Bitwarden logins fit the website, by name and user name, never a password. You approve one with your fingerprint, face or screen lock.
aOS on your Mac then gets exactly that login from Bitwarden and types it into the workspace. Neither the phone nor the Mac keeps it.
Without Bitwarden, your password app\'s autofill fills the fields in the request; aOS sends them once, encrypted over SSH, and doesn\'t keep them.
It asks for a sign-in by naming the site and why. You see the request and decide.
It never gets the password; it only learns whether the sign-in worked.
The phone reaches your Mac over SSH (the Mac\'s Remote Login), with a key made on this phone that never leaves it. The Mac\'s key is checked every time.
There is no server of ours in between. Outside your home network you need Tailscale or another VPN to reach the Mac.
The pictures of your Mac and the workspace travel through the same SSH connection and aren\'t stored.
The Mac account name and password for its screen stay on this phone, encrypted, and only go to the Mac\'s screen sharing.
aOS for Android contains Open Screen Sharing’s screen library, which is licensed under the GNU General Public License, version 3. So the app as a whole is licensed under it too.
You can get the source of this app and of the libraries in it from its author.

The screen of the workspace and of the Mac is based on Open Screen Sharing by nekohasekai, used under the GNU General Public License, version 3. aOS changed it for its own use: the screens are reached through the connection to your Mac, and aOS\'s sign-in replaces the app\'s own.
aOS is not made by the author of Open Screen Sharing and is not associated with it.
Source code of Open Screen Sharing
aOS\'s own Tailscale on this phone is Tailscale\'s open source code (tailscale.com), under the BSD 3-Clause License.
Apache MINA SSHD (the SSH connection), the terminal libraries of Termux (terminal-emulator, terminal-view), ZXing and ZXing Android Embedded (the QR scanner), AndroidX and Kotlin.
The phone tries the same network first, then the tailnet, then the Mac\'s name on the network.
Your Mac uses the Tailscale app. On this phone the Tailscale app, signed in with the same account, reaches it too; so does aOS\'s own Tailscale below.
No VPN and no Tailscale app needed. aOS only reaches your Mac through it, and nothing on this phone is reachable in your tailnet. Its keys stay on this phone, out of backups.
Your Mac uses aOS\'s own Tailscale. Set it up here too: you sign in once with your Tailscale account, the same as on the Mac.
aOS can bring Tailscale along on this phone too: no VPN, no extra app. You sign in once with your Tailscale account, the same as on the Mac.
Your Mac is in the tailnet %1$s. Sign out here and sign in with that account.
Sign in to Tailscale on the page that opened.
Signed in. The tailnet\'s admin still has to approve this phone in the Tailscale admin console.
Sign Out removes this phone from the tailnet and deletes its Tailscale keys here.

If you install the Tailscale app later and sign in with the same account, aOS\'s devices appear in the same tailnet, and you manage them there like any other device. The Tailscale app can\'t take over aOS\'s connection.
Sign out of Tailscale on this phone?
This phone leaves your tailnet. On the go it then reaches the Mac only through the Tailscale app, if it has it.
